newsitem.title: UK: Britons get fatter, but a little healthier - survey.
newsitem.headline: Britons get fatter, but a little healthier - survey.

text.p: Britons are getting fatter but their overall blood pressure has fallen a little, the government reported on Thursday.
In his annual survey on the state of the nation's health, Chief Medical Officer Kenneth Calman said 15 percent of men and 16.5 percent of women aged between 16 and 64 were obese.
This compared to 12.7 percent of men and 15 percent of women in 1991.
But while evidently ignoring exhortations to exercise more and eat less fat, Britons had at least managed to get their blood pressure down, Calman found.
He said the proportion of adults with high blood pressure fell from 24.2 percent to 22.4 percent between 1991 and 1995.
Mean systolic blood pressure -- the top number in a blood pressure reading -- fell from 139mmHg in 1991 to 136mmHg in 1995. The government target is 133mmHg by 2005.
High blood pressure is defined as 160 or higher.
"The overall reduction in average blood pressure between 1991 and 1995 is encouraging and future rounds of the survey will show if this is part of an ongoing trend," Calman said.

"If the improvement in treatment of high blood pressure also continues, this could cut the proportion of people who suffer from diseases such as stroke, for which hypertension is the main risk factor."
The survey also found that more people whose parents had smoked were themselves taking up the habit.
Among 16- to 24-year-olds, half of those whose parents smoked regularly now smoked themselves, compared to 26 percent of those whose parents did not smoke.
More than 16,000 adults and 3,700 children were questioned, weighed and had blood taken for the survey.
